text.p: The French franc led a fresh retreat from the mark in morning Europe, spooked by opinion polls predicting a wafer-thin majority for the centre right in France's forthcoming election and stirring fears about EMU.
An IPSOS poll for weekly Le Point saw the ruling coalition winning 292 seats in the 577-member national Assembly, with the Socialists on 256, Communists 28 and National Front one.

"It's a blow to EMU prospects, albeit a marginal one for now, and the knee-jerk reaction is a move back into the mark," said Ken Wattret, economist at Paribas. "Irrespective of any implications for EMU, it's clearly a negative for the franc."

Another survey, also released yesterday, showed 50 percent of those questioned believed EMU would not help economic growth and 69 percent favoured a new referendum on the euro. Over 70 percent thought the single currency would not help reduce unemployment or social inequalities.

Analysts said the immediate reaction to Monday's announcement of a snap election for May 25/June 1 had been sanguine, with the market expecting the status quo of an EMU-committed centre-right ruling coalition to be maintained.
The opinion polls had thrown those assumptions into question and threatened a rocky road to the election, they warned.

"The four weeks until the first round of polling are going to remain volatile, and probably provide an intermittent source of demand for marks," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
The franc eased to 3.3754/59 per mark by 0753 GMT from late Thursday's European level of 3.3744/49.

A more notable casualty, however, was the Italian lira, which has grown increasingly vulnerable to the market's EMU nerves. The lira was badly shaken this week when the European Commission predicted that Italy and Greece would be the only EU states to miss the deficit target for monetary union.
Italy holds local elections on Sunday, and voters were likely to deliver little cheer to Prime Minister Romano Prodi's troubled centre-left government, analysts said.
"They're not the kind of elections that can prompt a government collapse, but they should be prompting market jitters if it looks as if the PDS are losing ground," said Wattret.
The PDS (Democratic Party of the Left) is the biggest party in Italy's centre-left coalition.
Bundesbank council member Helmut Hesse said last night that EU political leaders had room to allow a small overshoot of the Maastricht Treaty's three percent deficit/GDP requirement.
"The deficit criterion will not be regarded as fulfilled or not fulfilled by looking at the statistics. It will be a political decision," Hesse told reporters.
But such comments are of little comfort to Italy, since the EU forecasts which projected its 1997 deficit at 3.2 percent are themselves seen as highly political, analysts said.
In its spring forecasts, released on Wednesday, the EU said Germany and France should hit the 3.0 percent goal, though the IMF later predicted even those EMU-lynchpins would overshoot.
One of Germany's "wise men" economic advisers said today that Germany was likely to miss the EMU entry criteria.
Juergen Donges told Reuters he saw no real chance for Germany to meet the criteria, both on deficit and debt levels.

The mark was also buoyed ahead of this weekend's Group of Seven meeting in Washington. The market is eager to see whether the G7 will attempt to rein in the dollar, although dollar/yen is seen as a greater cause of concern than dollar/mark.
Weakening of the dollar will remove another support from the mark's fragile European satellites, said analysts.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
